name: Inositol nicotinate
lead: Inositol nicotinate, also called inositol hexanicotinate or inositol hexaniacinate, is a compound formed from niacin (vitamin B3) and inositol. In the United States it is sold as a dietary supplement marketed as a "no-flush" form of niacin, and the body is described as breaking it down into its two components [1].

People who consider it for their appearance generally reach it through a circulation chain: niacin is a vasodilator, and inositol nicotinate has been studied for improving blood flow to the fingers and legs, so some users hope for warmer, better-perfused skin without the red flush that standard niacin produces. It is also taken in the same spirit as niacin for lipid profiles and general wellness, topics that gym and supplement forums such as T Nation discuss alongside diet and training [11][12].

Published research has focused on Raynaud's phenomenon and intermittent claudication rather than on skin, hair or facial appearance. Small thermographic and blood-flow studies from the late 1970s and early 1980s examined digital circulation [2][3][4], randomised trials in the 1980s examined walking distance [7][8], and a UK health technology assessment evaluated it alongside other drugs for claudication [5]. Wikipedia describes the evidence for most other proposed uses, including cholesterol lowering, as unclear or insufficient [1].

paras: The compound has been used for peripheral circulation disorders, notably Raynaud's phenomenon and intermittent claudication, and has also been promoted for cholesterol and blood pressure. Its effectiveness for high cholesterol, high blood pressure and exercise-related leg pain is described as unclear, with mixed study results [1]. Other proposed uses, such as migraine, psoriasis and restless legs syndrome, are described as lacking sufficient supporting evidence [1].

Raynaud's phenomenon is episodic vasospasm of the small vessels of the digits, causing white, blue and then red colour changes of the fingers or toes in response to cold or stress [6][7]. This visible skin-colour change, and the cold, pale hands that accompany it, is the closest link between the compound's studied uses and anything related to how the skin looks.

In forum discussion the compound appears mainly as a gentler alternative to niacin, taken with B-complex vitamins and fish oil in lipid-focused routines, and occasionally suggested for circulation complaints such as Raynaud's [11][12][13]. No source examined describes a skin, hair or facial-appearance trial.

Inositol nicotinate is an ester in which six nicotinic acid groups are attached to one inositol molecule. After ingestion it is reported to be metabolised to inositol and niacin. Wikipedia notes research suggesting that the absence of flushing may relate to limited conversion to active niacin [1]. Flushing is the skin warming and redness typical of immediate-release niacin.

A forum poster in a cognition-supplement thread reported that regular niacin appeared to do things that inositol hexanicotinate and niacinamide did not, which echoes the question of how much free niacin the ester releases [14]. A pharmacology thread on vasodilators lists the broad category of vasodilator drugs as biochemically heterogeneous [15].

Taken orally it is described as generally safe, with possible stomach upset, intestinal gas and nausea, and liver damage similar to other niacin products [1]. Cautions listed include diabetes (possible rise in blood sugar), liver or kidney disease, bleeding disorders or upcoming surgery, and gout [1].

Raynaud's phenomenon: a 1977 study used quantitative thermography to compare hand temperature in normal controls and rheumatoid patients with Raynaud's. Oral inositol nicotinate (Hexopal) was followed by an initial rise in a thermographic index of the hand and fingers, after which temperature fell and then rose again after a period of weeks [4]. A 1979 randomised, controlled evaluation in thirty patients with primary and secondary Raynaud's used several non-invasive techniques, including the time needed to induce an attack and total and nutrient digital blood flow, and reported significant beneficial effects as well as a prolonged build-up period before the drug took effect [8]. A further thermal-imaging study appeared in 1981 [9]. Narrative reviews of Raynaud's treatment and a BMJ Clinical Evidence summary of secondary Raynaud's discuss the drug class among treatment options [6][10].

Intermittent claudication: two randomised controlled trials of Hexopal in intermittent claudication were published in the British Journal of Clinical Practice in 1988 [16][17]. A 2011 health technology assessment evaluated cilostazol, naftidrofuryl oxalate, pentoxifylline and inositol nicotinate against no vasoactive drug for claudication in peripheral arterial disease, looking at walking distance, ankle-brachial index, adverse events and quality of life [5].

Lipids and other uses: German-language trials from the 1970s tested inositol nicotinate in combination with clofibrate for hyperlipoproteinaemia [18], and a 1966 Nordic trial examined it in peripheral arterial insufficiency [19].
No studies found that examine inositol nicotinate for skin, hair or facial appearance.

Inositol nicotinate is sold without prescription in the US as a supplement, and Hexopal is a branded product [1]. On T Nation, contributors have discussed it among niacin forms: one poster recommended it as a no-flush niacin alongside a B-complex for a low HDL reading [12], while another wrote that over-the-counter niacinamide or inositol hexanicotinate does nothing for lipid modification and that prescription extended-release niacin would be needed [13]. A 2002 thread on Raynaud's listed inositol nicotinate and nicotinic acid among forms of vitamin B3 that relax smooth muscle in vessels [11].

card.summary: A no-flush niacin ester sold as a supplement; studied for circulation, with nothing published on appearance.
card.note: Evidence is limited to small circulation studies; liver effects are listed as for other niacin products.

quick.overview:
Inositol nicotinate is niacin bound to inositol, sold as a supplement that does not cause the usual niacin flush. It is included in appearance catalogues because of its niacin link.

Published research concerns circulation (Raynaud's phenomenon, leg pain on walking) and has produced mixed or unclear results. Nothing found examines skin or looks outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It is described as being broken down into inositol and niacin after ingestion; limited conversion to active niacin may explain the lack of flushing.
quick.risks: Generally described as safe orally, with stomach upset, gas, nausea and possible liver effects similar to other niacin products. Cautions are listed for diabetes, liver or kidney disease, bleeding disorders and gout. Sold over the counter in the US.

chain: Ester of niacin and inositol is broken down after ingestion
Niacin component acts as a vasodilator without the typical flush
Possible warmer, better-perfused skin and extremities
angle.text: Users interested in niacin's circulatory and skin-related associations choose this form because it is reported not to cause the red, warm flush of immediate-release niacin. Its measured effects in studies concern blood flow in the fingers and legs, and no published study reports skin or facial outcomes.
